s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 Aug 2026
m: Published Forbes real-time list figure
did: An accountant for small Southwest refineries, he and partners bought bankrupt El Paso Refining in 1992, took full control five years later, renamed it Western Refining, listed it in 2006 and sold it to Tesoro in 2017 for 6.4 billion dollars.
why: No new US refinery had been permitted since 1976, so refining capacity was a closed set. Buying a shuttered plant at scrap value and restarting it created capacity nobody could rebuild, and El Paso sat on the only pipeline route into a landlocked market with no competing supply.
obst: The plant he bought had been idled and stripped in bankruptcy and he had never run one. The 2008 crash landed right after he paid 1.5 billion dollars for Giant Industries, and Western Refining traded under 4 dollars a share while carrying that debt.
turn: The 2003 purchase of the Bloomfield and Ciniza refineries in New Mexico, which turned a single-plant operator into a regional system with pipeline reach.

s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 Aug 2026

did: Welded a pot still out of turkey-fryer pots in a field east of Austin in 1997, took the first legal distilling permit in Texas, and grew Titos Handmade Vodka past 12 million cases a year while never selling a share of it.
why: He took no outside capital and never sold, so every dollar of a category carrying 60 percent gross margin stayed with one owner. Corn-based and gluten-free let him win shelf space against imports whose only real advantage was European provenance.
obst: He funded the first years on about 90,000 dollars drawn across 19 credit cards and slept at the distillery; distributors would not return calls until a medal forced them to, and a 2014 class action attacked the handmade wording on the label.
turn: Winning double gold at the 2001 San Francisco World Spirits Competition against 71 other vodkas, which turned a local curiosity into a brand distributors would carry.

s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 Aug 2026

did: Grew his family grocery distributor in Temple about 30 percent a year for three decades into a national convenience-store supply business, sold McLane Company to Sam Walton in 1991 for 50 million dollars plus 10.4 million Walmart shares, then owned the Houston Astros from 1992 to 2011.
why: He took the 1991 payment in Walmart stock rather than cash exactly as Walmart began its national build-out, so the sale price compounded with the buyer. The distribution business itself won on route density, serving convenience stores too small for grocery wholesalers to reach profitably.
obst: He inherited a thin-margin regional wholesaler with no capital. The Astros lost money in the Astrodome and he threatened to move the franchise to Virginia in 1995 before Houston voters approved a downtown ballpark.
turn: Structuring the 1991 Walmart sale largely in stock, which converted a 50 million dollar business into a position that compounded for a decade.

s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 Aug 2026

It has raised 615 million dollars at a 10.32 billion dollar valuation, after he had already sold five earlier startups including Hypergiant to Thrive Capital in 2023.
why: He priced a research programme as a venture asset by attaching it to specific nameable species, which produced continuous global press and let him raise at software multiples for wet-lab biology. The gene-editing and biobanking tools license into conservation whether or not a mammoth ever walks.
obst: Conservation biologists publicly called de-extinction a distraction from funding for living species, and the 2025 dire wolf announcement drew accusations that the animals were edited grey wolves, forcing the company to defend its species definition in public.
turn: The April 2025 dire wolf announcement, which took the valuation from roughly 1.5 billion dollars to over 10 billion within months.

why: Palantir sold classified-grade data integration to agencies that could not buy it any other way, and holding founder stock through a 2020 direct listing converted sixteen years of illiquidity into public equity. 8VC recycles that into defense procurement, where a few new entrants can capture programme budgets that used to be closed.
obst: A former intern sued him for sexual assault in 2015 and Stanford briefly barred him from campus; the suit was dropped in 2016 with a retraction, but limited partners and portfolio boards kept their distance through the year it ran.
turn: Palantirs September 2020 direct listing, which finally made a sixteen-year-old private position sellable.

why: She bet the company on one new x86 microarchitecture and on outsourcing manufacture to TSMC while Intel stayed vertically integrated. When Intels 10nm process slipped for years, the fabless model let AMD ship on the leading node and take datacenter share Intel could not defend.
obst: AMD had negative free cash flow, about 2.2 billion dollars of debt and a share price under 2 dollars in 2015; she sold a majority of the Malaysian and Chinese assembly plants to raise cash while analysts modelled bankruptcy.
turn: The March 2017 launch of Ryzen on the Zen core, the first AMD part in a decade that matched Intel on per-core performance.

why: Drive priced credit for borrowers banks would not score and funded it through securitisation, so the spread was captured at origination and the credit risk sold on. When Santander wanted a US consumer platform it had to buy an operator that already held the dealer relationships.
obst: State attorneys general pursued Santander Consumer over subprime underwriting and it paid a 26 million dollar multistate settlement; his 2015 exit followed a Federal Reserve objection to the parent banks capital plan.
turn: The January 2014 IPO of Santander Consumer USA, which put a public price on his stake and set up the cash exit a year later.

s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 Aug 2026, No. 2052

why: The Barnett Shale needed pressure-pumping horsepower years before the service majors built it, and the Wilks brothers owned the sand, the pumps and the trucks outright rather than leasing them. When day rates spiked from 2008 to 2010 the whole margin fell to equity instead of to lessors.
obst: They had no oilfield background and financed the first trucks against a masonry business. Idaho and Montana ranchers and conservation groups fought their land buying, and ProFrac shares fell more than 80 percent after the 2022 IPO as frac pricing collapsed.
turn: The 2011 sale of Frac Tech to the Temasek-led consortium, timed at the peak of the first shale service cycle.

s: Forbes Real-Time Billionaires profile, 21 Aug 2026, No. 2174

why: He owned the entire company by the time salsa passed ketchup as Americas top condiment, and Campbell could not build a challenger brand fast enough to catch a name already on the shelf. Buying the other half at a 1987 private mark captured all of the revaluation that followed.
obst: The 1987 divorce forced a buyout he had to finance against the company itself, and litigation over the 95 million dollar valuation followed once the Campbell sale printed 1.1 billion seven years later.
turn: The 1987 buyout of his ex-wifes interest, which converted a shared family holding into sole ownership just before the salsa category tripled.

obst: Crescent carried heavy debt into the 1998 REIT selloff and the stock lost more than half its value; the 2009 buyback had to be negotiated with Barclays as lender on a portfolio that was underwater.
turn: The August 2007 sale of Crescent to Morgan Stanley, closed weeks before the credit markets shut.

obst: He carried the acreage through the 2015 and 2016 crash when Permian private operators were being pushed into distressed sales, and his political spending made him a target of Texas House inquiries and a 2024 defamation suit from a former legislator.
turn: Occidentals December 2023 agreement to buy CrownRock for 12 billion dollars.

why: The 1984 AT and T breakup made wholesale minutes available to any reseller, so the binding constraint was customer acquisition. obst: State regulators pursued Excel over slamming complaints generated by its agent network, underwriters balked at the multilevel model before the listing, and he was paid in Teleglobe stock in 1998 and had to work out of it before that company collapsed in 2002.
turn: The May 1996 NYSE listing, at the time the largest US IPO by a company selling through a commission-only agent force.

why: Tricon buys and physically moves petrochemicals between producing and consuming regions, so its margin comes from logistics and credit rather than from price direction. Owning the storage, the chartering and the receivables lets it serve buyers in markets producers will not sell to directly.
obst: The family paper and newspaper businesses were wiped out in the 1970s recession, forcing the move to Brazil, and he has had to fund a physical trading book on bank lines that are the first thing withdrawn in every commodity downturn.
turn: The 1996 founding of Tricon in Houston, which put him at the pipe end of the US Gulf Coast petrochemical build just as export volumes began.

why: Captive agents can quote only one carrier, so Goosehead built a network that quotes dozens and keeps the renewal commission. obst: Carriers refused appointments to a new agency with no book, so early growth depended on a handful of regional insurers; after the IPO the shares fell more than 70 percent from their 2021 high as Texas homeowners carriers pulled capacity and non-renewed policies.
turn: The 2011 decision to franchise rather than hire agents, which turned one office into a national network without adding corporate payroll.

obst: The company nearly ran out of cash in 2001 when the dot-com bust took its customers and he had to personally guarantee payroll; after the 2008 IPO priced at 12.50 dollars the stock halved within months, and AWS price cuts eventually forced the sale to Apollo.

obst: Overseas factories copied the rotomoulded design within two years and YETI fought a long run of patent and trade-dress suits including against RTIC; a 2023 recall of about 1.9 million soft coolers and gear cases over magnet ingestion hit during a wholesale slowdown.

s: SEC beneficial ownership for Cactus Inc (WHD) compiled Aug 2026: Cactus WH Enterprises LLC, the Bender family vehicle, held 9,261,249 shares valued at 683 million dollars

why: Cactus rents its wellheads and services them with its own field crews, so it earns a day rate on installed iron rather than a one-time sale and the same tree is re-rented across dozens of wells. That converts a capital good into recurring revenue and makes the business far less cyclical than pressure pumping.
obst: They launched in 2011 against integrated majors who bundled wellheads free with pumping contracts and had to prove the rental model one operator at a time; the 2020 collapse cut US frac crews by three quarters and the shares fell under 12 dollars.
turn: The February 2018 NYSE listing, which funded the FlexSteel acquisition and turned a private rental fleet into a consolidator.

s: Forbes profile figure last updated 28 May 2024; she retains an 18 percent Bumble stake

why: Dating apps are two-sided markets that fail when women churn, and making women initiate removed the unsolicited-message problem that drove them off rival apps. That retention advantage cut paid acquisition cost per active woman, the only genuinely scarce side of the market.
obst: She left Tinder in 2014 after a harassment suit settled without admission; Bumble stock then fell roughly 90 percent from its 2021 debut, she stepped down as chief executive in January 2024 and had to return fourteen months later to a shrinking paying user base.
turn: The February 2021 Nasdaq IPO at 43 dollars a share, which valued Bumble at about 8.2 billion dollars.

turn: ExxonMobils December 2009 agreement to buy XTO for about 41 billion dollars in stock, the largest US onshore deal of the shale era.

s: SEC beneficial ownership for Vital Farms (VITL) compiled Aug 2026: 12,640,310 shares, 29.44 percent, valued at 137 million dollars
m: Disclosed share count times implied market price
did: Started Vital Farms in 2007 on a 27-acre farm outside Austin with 20 hens, built a contracted network of more than 300 family farms each giving hens 108 square feet of pasture, and listed the company on Nasdaq in 2020; it now sells the leading US pasture-raised egg brand.
why: Eggs are a commodity priced by the case, so he moved the product out of the commodity by defining and auditing a standard, 108 square feet per bird, that no cage-free competitor could claim. That certification held a retail price two to three times conventional, and contracting the farms rather than owning them kept the capital off his.
obst: Avian influenza killed tens of millions of US laying hens in 2015 and again from 2022 to 2025, forcing repeated supply shortfalls, and a 2021 class action challenged whether the pasture-raised and ethical claims on the carton matched conditions on contract farms.
turn: The 2010 national listing with Whole Foods, which took one Austin farms eggs into a chain with a store in every affluent US metro.

s: Aggregated SEC Form 4 and Schedule 13 insider holdings as of March 2026, totalling at least 141 million dollars
m: SEC filing aggregate of disclosed public-company holdings; excludes private assets and prior cash proceeds
did: A lawyer turned dealmaker who took over the dairy Suiza in a 100 million dollar leveraged buyout in 1993, listed it in 1996, rolled up the fragmented US fluid milk industry past 6 billion dollars of revenue, merged with Dean Foods in a 2.5 billion dollar deal in 2001, spun out WhiteWave in 2012 and sold it to Danone for 12.5 billion.
why: Fluid milk is bulky, perishable and cannot be shipped far, so every metro had a local processor with no exit. Buying them one at a time with public equity acquired regional monopolies at private multiples and consolidated plant and freight overhead, while the Dean name gave the scale to negotiate with national grocery chains.
obst: The Dean merger drew a Justice Department antitrust suit that forced divestitures, dairy farmer groups sued over Southeast milk pricing, and the legacy fluid milk business he left behind filed for bankruptcy in 2019.
turn: The 2012 spin-off of WhiteWave, which separated growing organic and plant-based brands from a declining fluid milk business and made the Danone sale possible.
